Narrative: During preparations for installing a 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
What_Went_Wrong: The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with no effective barrier against dropped objects.
Corrective_Actions: All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier (e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project- wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

Narrative: Loss of containment of 27 m3 of oily water (Water phase: 22,140 kg + Oil phase: 4,323 kg = Total: 26,463 kg), through the top valve of the port Slop tank of the FPSO, during an operation to receive oily water resulting from the backwashing of the offloading hoses.
What_Went_Wrong: ? The port slop tank overflow was caused by a combination of factors. First, the high-high level alarm set point was incorrect, allowing the tank to overflow without the alarm being activated. In addition, there were intermittent failures in the high-level sensor, which did not function when required. The investigation showed a history of spurious activation of this alarm, as well as revealed that the contractor did not implement a decision-making 117 criterion in cases of reaching critical levels of the slop tanks, following a similar accident in 2022, which could have prevented the occurrence. Finally, the control methodology was flawed, as there was no robust system to ensure that the dump valve remained closed, in deviation from the guidelines of the operational procedure, which could have mitigated the overflow.
Corrective_Actions: Correct the virtual high-level alarm set for the port and starboard slop tank to a level below the drop line nozzle with a lock for manual adjustment. Correct the set point for the very high-level alarms for the port and starboard slop vessels, keeping it below the drop line nozzle level. Perform maintenance on the port slop high-level alarm, ensuring its operability. Perform tests on the other level alarms for the tanks and vessels in the open drainage system, and perform maintenance on the sensors that are not fully operational. Create a maintenance plan for calibrating the level sensor for the open drainage tanks. Review the related operating procedure and train the team on the updated version. Implement a reliable system for controlling the opening and closing of the dump valves, with leadership signatures. Narrative: Collision between northern crane and derrick resulting in falling objects.
What_Went_Wrong: Three objects fell after the north crane collided with the derrick. The crane operator had been planning to perform lubrication of the slewing ring with the logistics discipline responsible for some time, but this was changed to the crane operator bringing along a deck operator who was being trained as a crane-operator. A helicopter was on its way to the platform, and they had about 25 minutes to finish before the helicopter arrived. It was decided that the crane operator was to perform the lubrication in the crane pedestal while the deck operator operated the crane. The crane was lifted and swung out over the sea. The crane operator reminded to "elevate the crane-boom" to avoid the derrick and then went down into the pedestal. The deck operator elevated the boom and swung the crane towards the platform. After a brief stop to change the lubrication cartridge, the crane was topped up a little more before it swung further towards the derrick. The deck operator believed the boom was topped up enough. The walkway and the spotlight mounted on the right side of the boom were driven into the upper corner of the wind wall high up in the derrick. At the same time, the crane was lifted somewhat and detached from the tower. The crane shook, and the deck operator observed an object fall into an area where personnel were normally present. After receiving information about what had happened over the radio, the crane operator came to the cabin, took over, and lowered the crane into the cradle. The logistics discipline responsible heard what was being said on the radio, responded, and found the spotlight in a pallet with wooden lids in the moonpool area. Narrative: On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in the laundry. Narrative: While running the Upper Completion into the hole, the personnel on the rig floor heard something fall. Rig floor operations were suspended immediately to investigate the cause of the sound. The HPU (Hydraulic Power Unit) located at the rear of the drill floor was observed to be missing one of its access doors. Nobody was injured and no damage caused to any other equipment because of this incident. The operation was stopped immediately, and the crews conducted a safety stand down – proceeded to check on all the doors on the rig floor to ensure all were properly secured, checked security of the handrails on stairs, and checked for any other loose objects on drill floor. The door landed near the High Pressure (HP) Kill Line, so the entire Kill Line was inspected. No HP Kill Line equipment was damaged. Narrative: Five crew members were in the process of measuring 13 5/8” casing joints on the main deck of the drilling rig. Three crew members were on the port side and two on the starboard side. The casing was placed on top of the rack and spread out. The port side crew members used a rope to roll one joint at a time towards the aft of the rig with the assistance of the starboard crew member who pushed the pipe to give it a start. Once a joint was stopped, a crew member on either side would back the thread protectors off before rolling the next joint of casing. The injured person (IP) was on the starboard side backing out the box protector on one of the casing joints when another casing joint was rolled toward him. The IP’s right index finger was caught between the two joints of casing. His injury resulted in a medevac and subsequent amputation of the finger.
What_Went_Wrong: The work instruction did not adequately detail steps for the job and the risks of rolling joints and removing casing protectors were not captured; the crew attempted to improve the process of strapping joints using rope, however, the risks introduced by this method were not adequately assessed. The casing had been previously measured onshore. Due to inaccuracies seen in previous onshore measurements a decision was made to strap every joint offshore at the rig-site. A breakdown in communication led to IP’s hands being in the Line of Fire. He was in the process of backing off the box protector using his hands when another crew member rolled the casing onto his hand.
Corrective_Actions: 1. Critical review of lower risk activities on sites which can result in life changing injury (LCI)/fatalities 2. Eliminate/minimize normalization of hand injury line of fire risks.

Narrative: At approximately 04:45, the bonnet holding bolts for a 2-inch globe valve, operating at 960psi, failed, resulting in a gas release. An emergency shutdown was initiated, and the platform was safely de-pressured. Once the gas had dissipated, the investigation team found that the actuator and other components had been dislodged, causing damage to the piping and cooling fans above. The actuator was found ~5ft away from valve body location with other components up to 25ft away. Cause of valve failure was CSCC (chloride stress corrosion cracking) of SS304 bolts.
What_Went_Wrong: • Project documentation did not prohibit the use of SS304 materials – they were “not recommended”. • Project Quality controls did not prevent delivery and installation of a valve with SS304 bolts that were stated in supplier documentation to be SS316. • Operations integrity management documentation did not provide guidance for inspection of stainless-steel materials. • Inspection and replacement campaigns resulting from past SS304 failure events had a narrow focus and so failed to identify full scope of the risk.
Corrective_Actions: • Update Project standards to require that stainless steel fasteners must have ≥ 2% Mo content. • Update the procedure to provide guidance on stainless steel inspection and also include inspection of all stainless-steel bolting in the inspection contractor’s scope. • Conduct gas detector coverage modelling to confirm existing gas detectors provide sufficient coverage. • All assets: review SS304 risk and create action plan to manage this.

Narrative: Sludge flow through the side valve of the head in an uncontrolled manner, while the insulation pipe packoff was being installed. It is a High Potential Event. One of the side valves in section B of the wellhead must be open during the lowering of the packer, according to the procedure of the supplier company. The well “recovers” energy due to a degradation of the fluid barrier (loss of level in the well), which produces an uncontrolled upwelling for approximately 1 hour. It is possible to close the well in a “manual” way by operating the flywheel of this valve. Final state of packer out of position. The packing procedure should be revised to take into account situations of unstable well and degradation of the primary barrier (sludge).
